steps.title: Layers that matter
steps.desc: OSI / TCP-IP as an attacker reads them

blocks.text: You don't debug "the internet." You debug which layer failed — name, port, route, or cable.
L7 Application HTTP · DNS · TLS · SSH
L4 Transport TCP · UDP · ports
L3 Network IP · ICMP · routing
L2 Data link MAC · ARP · Ethernet
L1 Physical cable · Wi‑Fi · NIC
Symptom

items: Site loads forever → often DNS or TCP
Connection refused → port closed / no listener
Timeout → filter, blackhole, or no route

blocks.text: First question

items: Is the port open from here?
Do I have a route to that IP?

quiz.q: curl returns "Could not resolve host". Which layer broke first?

options.why: Name → IP failed. DNS is application-layer naming before TCP even starts.
Routing needs a destination IP; DNS never produced one.
You never reached TCP — no IP to connect to yet.
Physical is fine if the NIC works — you never got an IP from DNS.

steps.title: Your host on the wire

blocks.text: Every box needs an IP (L3), a MAC (L2), and usually a default gateway to leave the LAN.

items: Gateway — first hop off your subnet
ARP — IP → MAC on the local segment

blocks.text: In the lab: Target: your own laptop / VM

quiz.q: Two PCs on the same /24 talk. ARP is used to find…

options.text: The MAC address for a neighbor IP
options.why: On the LAN, frames need a MAC. ARP answers “who has this IP?”

options.text: The DNS server for that subnet
options.why: DNS maps names to IPs — not MACs.
Public IP of the ISP is not what ARP resolves locally.

steps.title: Subnets & CIDR
steps.desc: Who can talk without a router

blocks.text: CIDR says how many bits are network vs host. Same network bits → same LAN → no router needed.
Address Meaning Attack note
172.16.0.0/12 Private Common in corp / cloud VPC
192.168.0.0/16 Private Home / small office
127.0.0.1 Loopback Local-only services
Quick math
→ network , broadcast , usable . Host is a different subnet.

quiz.q: Host A is 10.0.0.50/24. Host B is 10.0.1.50/24. To talk, they need…

options.why: Different third octet under /24 ⇒ different subnets. A router (or L3 switch) must forward.
/24 means third octet is network — 10.0.0 vs 10.0.1 are different LANs.
ARP only works inside one L2/L3 segment — not across /24 boundaries.
